lesson.title: What Stays, What Goes: Introns and Exons
lesson.summary: Exons are the sequences within a gene that are kept and expressed in the mature mRNA, while introns are the intervening sequences that get removed during splicing.
lesson.body:
The splicing process removes something and keeps something else, and those two categories have names: introns are the intervening sequences that get cut out, and exons are the sequences that remain and are eventually expressed as protein. The terms were coined by molecular biologist Walter Gilbert, exon for expressed sequence and intron for intragenic sequence, and the names still capture the distinction well: exons exit the nucleus as part of the mature message, while introns stay behind, get degraded, and never make it into the cytoplasm.

Within a single gene, exons and introns typically alternate multiple times along the DNA, so the region coding for one protein is actually built from several separate blocks rather than one continuous stretch. In many human genes, the total length taken up by introns is considerably larger than the length taken up by the exons that will actually survive into the mature mRNA, meaning a large fraction of what RNA polymerase transcribes never appears in the final message at all.

It is tempting to think of introns as wasted effort, but that is not quite accurate. Some introns contain regulatory sequences that influence when or how much a gene is expressed, and some host smaller RNA genes within their boundaries. Most importantly for the chapters that follow, the fact that a gene's coding information is split into discrete, separable exon blocks is exactly what makes it possible for a cell to include some exons in one mature mRNA and different exons in another, from the very same gene and the very same pre-mRNA. That flexibility, built directly on the intron-exon structure described here and the cutting-and-rejoining chemistry of splicing, is what alternative splicing takes advantage of next.
